blocker_history.summary: Two independent agent sessions failed to reach the deployed database. Attempt 1 tried three routes (direct env read, sandboxed read, a runner using the toolkit's own alloy_load_trusted_server_env_exports). Attempt 2 tried four more and established that TWO independent controls were in play — a workspace boundary refusing any read outside the worktree, and command approval — so lifting either alone would not have worked.
blocker_history.structural_finding: DATABASE_URL is on the toolkit's explicit denylist twice: as a secret-like substring (scripts/local-dev/lib/verify.sh:202) and as a named privileged variable (:210). Its only reader is alloy_load_trusted_server_env_exports (:495-523), which exists solely to spawn the alloy-dev-start Next process. The refusal was working as designed.
blocker_history.resolution: The trusted host action (database.read_census) is the correct answer and the one worth reusing: the Director executes privileged reads host-side and returns only results, so the worker never holds a credential and the denylist is never weakened. Every future live-evidence step in this programme — including re-running this census before each lockout-class switch, and the §11 migration preflights, all of which require read-only queries against the same database — should use this channel rather than asking an operator to paste anything.

queries.question: Is handle_new_user() attached to auth.users?
queries.sql:
SELECT t.tgname, t.tgenabled, t.tgisinternal, p.proname AS function_name
FROM pg_trigger t
JOIN pg_proc p ON p.oid = t.tgfoid
WHERE t.tgrelid = 'auth.users'::regclass
ORDER BY t.tgname;
queries.supporting_sql:
SELECT n.nspname, p.proname
FROM pg_proc p
JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = p.pronamespace
WHERE p.proname = 'handle_new_user';
queries.reading: tgisinternal = true rows are FK/constraint triggers, not application triggers — exclude them when judging. A non-internal, enabled ('O' or 'A') trigger naming handle_new_user means G1 is LIVE: every new auth user silently receives a default role, and W-20 rises into wave 2.

result.answer: handle_new_user() is DEFINED but NOT ATTACHED to auth.users.
result.verdict: G1 is LATENT, not live. All 62 triggers on auth.users are tgisinternal=true referential-integrity triggers (RI_ConstraintTrigger_*, running RI_FKey_cascade_del / RI_FKey_noaction_upd / RI_FKey_setnull_del / RI_FKey_noaction_del). Zero application triggers exist, so no new auth user currently receives a default role by trigger. The total rose from 54 at run 1 purely because new migrations added foreign keys referencing auth.users; the application-trigger count — the only figure Q1's rule reads — is 0 in both runs.
result.consequence: The plan §4 rule 'a non-zero Q1 promotes G1 from latent to live and moves W-20 into wave 2' DOES NOT FIRE. W-20 stays in wave 5.
result.residual_hazard: The function still exists (1 definition) with no trigger referencing it. An unattached trigger function named handle_new_user is a loaded gun: any migration or dashboard action that attaches it silently restores the default-to-ops escalation path G1 describes, and nothing in the codebase would flag it. W-20 should give it an explicit disposition — drop it, or document why it is retained — rather than leaving it defined and unreferenced. This is a finding only Wave 0 could produce: version control shows the function, never its attachment.

queries.question: How many principals authorize ONLY via the legacy fallback (user_profiles / app_users) with no user_roles row?
queries.sql:
WITH no_membership AS (
  SELECT u.id AS user_id
  FROM auth.users u
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.user_roles ur WHERE ur.user_id = u.id)
),
legacy AS (
  SELECT
    nm.user_id,
    (SELECT up.role::text FROM public.user_profiles up WHERE up.id = nm.user_id) AS profile_role,
    COALESCE(
      (SELECT au.org_id FROM public.app_users au WHERE au.id = nm.user_id AND au.org_id IS NOT NULL LIMIT 1),
      (SELECT au.org_id FROM public.app_users au WHERE au.auth_user_id = nm.user_id AND au.org_id IS NOT NULL LIMIT 1)
    ) AS resolved_org_id,
    COALESCE(
      (SELECT au.role FROM public.app_users au WHERE au.id = nm.user_id LIMIT 1),
      (SELECT au.role FROM public.app_users au WHERE au.auth_user_id = nm.user_id LIMIT 1)
    ) AS app_user_role
  FROM no_membership nm
)
SELECT
  count(*) AS principals_without_membership,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE profile_role IN ('admin','ops') AND resolved_org_id IS NOT NULL) AS via_user_profiles,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE app_user_role IN ('admin','ops') AND resolved_org_id IS NOT NULL) AS via_app_users,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE (profile_role IN ('admin','ops') OR app_user_role IN ('admin','ops')) AND resolved_org_id IS NOT NULL) AS legacy_only_authorized
FROM legacy;
queries.detail_sql:
-- Per-principal disposition, for the remediation list if legacy_only_authorized > 0.
WITH no_membership AS (
  SELECT u.id AS user_id, u.email
  FROM auth.users u
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public.user_roles ur WHERE ur.user_id = u.id)
)
SELECT
  nm.user_id,
  (SELECT up.role::text FROM public.user_profiles up WHERE up.id = nm.user_id) AS profile_role,
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT au.org_id FROM public.app_users au WHERE au.id = nm.user_id AND au.org_id IS NOT NULL LIMIT 1),
    (SELECT au.org_id FROM public.app_users au WHERE au.auth_user_id = nm.user_id AND au.org_id IS NOT NULL LIMIT 1)
  ) AS resolved_org_id,
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT au.role FROM public.app_users au WHERE au.id = nm.user_id LIMIT 1),
    (SELECT au.role FROM public.app_users au WHERE au.auth_user_id = nm.user_id LIMIT 1)
  ) AS app_user_role
FROM no_membership nm
ORDER BY resolved_org_id NULLS LAST;
caveats: The product uses maybeSingle() on the app_users lookups, so a principal matching MORE THAN ONE app_users row errors at runtime rather than resolving. This census uses LIMIT 1 and will count such a principal as authorized. If legacy_only_authorized > 0, check for duplicate app_users rows per principal before designing W-20's remediation.

legacy_only_authorized is the L4 lockout population: these principals lose ALL authority the moment the fallback is deleted. It is NOT the sum of via_user_profiles and via_app_users — the two overlap.

result.answer: Zero. No principal authorizes only through the legacy fallback.
result.verdict: The L4 lockout population is EMPTY. Every auth user has at least one user_roles row, so the legacy fallback in resolveAdminAccessCore.ts:111-140 — which fires only when a principal has zero user_roles rows — is unreachable for every principal alive in this database today.
result.consequence: The plan §4 rule 'if Q2 > 0 the corresponding workstream gains a remediation step' DOES NOT FIRE. W-20 needs no remediation migration. Because the population is zero rather than merely small, W-20 collapses from the full four-step switch ritual to a straight deletion plus its tier A/B regression locks (RL-12).
result.caveat_now_moot: The duplicate-app_users-row caveat (the product uses maybeSingle(), which errors on more than one match, while this census used LIMIT 1) cannot bite: it applies only to principals with no membership row, and there are none.

queries.question: How many user_roles.role values have no role_definitions row for that org?
queries.sql:
SELECT
  count(*) AS undefined_membership_rows,
  count(DISTINCT ur.org_id) AS orgs_affected,
  count(DISTINCT ur.role) AS distinct_undefined_roles
FROM public.user_roles ur
LEFT JOIN public.role_definitions rd
  ON rd.org_id = ur.org_id AND rd.role_key = ur.role
WHERE rd.id IS NULL;
queries.detail_sql:
SELECT ur.org_id, ur.role, count(*) AS membership_rows
FROM public.user_roles ur
LEFT JOIN public.role_definitions rd
  ON rd.org_id = ur.org_id AND rd.role_key = ur.role
WHERE rd.id IS NULL
GROUP BY ur.org_id, ur.role
ORDER BY membership_rows DESC;
caveats: The anti-join ignores role_definitions.is_active on purpose: a foreign key does not care whether the referenced row is active. Q5 reads the same join with is_active, because a grant does.
undefined_membership_rows is exactly the set that would fail M9's FK, and therefore exactly the subject of M8's remediation migration.

result.answer: Zero. Every user_roles.role value has a matching role_definitions row for its org.
result.verdict: The L3 lockout population is EMPTY. No membership row would violate the FK.
result.consequence: The plan §4 rule 'if Q3 > 0, M8 is required and its row count must equal this number' DOES NOT FIRE. M8 (remediate undefined user_roles.role values) is NOT REQUIRED and is removed from the §11 register. M9 (the FK itself) can be applied directly, with a zero-violating-rows preflight expected to pass on the first attempt.
result.caution: Q3 deliberately ignores role_definitions.is_active, because a foreign key does not. That is the correct reading for M9. Q5 reads the same join WITH is_active because a grant does care. Both returned zero, so the distinction did not change the answer here — but M9's preflight must keep using Q3's form, not Q5's.

queries.question: How many memberships lack an access profile?
queries.sql:
WITH membership_pairs AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ur.user_id, ur.org_id FROM public.user_roles ur
)
SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM membership_pairs) AS distinct_user_org_pairs,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM public.user_roles) AS membership_rows,
  count(*) AS pairs_without_profile,
  count(DISTINCT mp.org_id) AS orgs_affected
FROM membership_pairs mp
LEFT JOIN public.user_access_profiles p
  ON p.user_id = mp.user_id AND p.org_id = mp.org_id
WHERE p.id IS NULL;
queries.supporting_sql:
-- The reverse direction: profile rows with no membership (orphans M1 must not touch).
SELECT count(*) AS profiles_without_membership
FROM public.user_access_profiles p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM public.user_roles ur
  WHERE ur.user_id = p.user_id AND ur.org_id = p.org_id
);
caveats: GRAIN MATTERS. user_roles is per (user, org, role) — the composite PK admits several rows per pair — while user_access_profiles is UNIQUE (user_id, org_id). M1's preflight rule 'row count == W-0 Q4' means pairs_without_profile, NOT membership_rows. Comparing against the wrong number makes the preflight pass on a wrong migration.
pairs_without_profile is the fail-open population: today each of these principals silently resolves to department_scope = all and site_scope = all.

result.answer: Two (user, org) pairs lack an access profile.
result.verdict: This is the ONLY non-empty lockout-class population, and it is the confirmed fail-open defect. 2 of 6 membership pairs currently resolve silently to department_scope = all AND site_scope = all via resolveAdminAccessCore.ts:144-162.
result.grain_ruling: THREE different numbers are in play — 8 membership rows, 6 distinct (user, org) pairs, 2 pairs without a profile. M1's preflight rule 'row count == W-0 Q4' means 2, the pairs_without_profile figure. Using 8 or 6 would let the preflight pass on a wrong migration. This is exactly the grain confusion flagged when the query was written; the live numbers now make it load-bearing rather than theoretical, because all three values are distinct.
result.consequence: The plan §4 rule 'if Q4 > 0' FIRES. M1 is sized at exactly 2 inserted rows. W-7 (absent scope denies) cannot precede M1.
result.bonus_finding: profiles_without_membership = 0 — there are no orphan profile rows, so M1's 'no existing profile row modified' preflight condition has nothing to collide with.

queries.question: Does every org holding an admin/ops membership have the matching role_definitions row?
queries.sql:
WITH admin_ops_pairs AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ur.org_id, ur.role
  FROM public.user_roles ur
  WHERE ur.role IN ('admin','ops')
)
SELECT
  count(*) AS admin_ops_org_role_pairs,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE rd.id IS NULL) AS pairs_with_no_definition,
  count(*) FILTER (WHERE rd.id IS NOT NULL AND rd.is_active IS FALSE) AS pairs_defined_but_inactive,
  count(DISTINCT aop.org_id) FILTER (WHERE rd.id IS NULL) AS orgs_at_lockout_risk
FROM admin_ops_pairs aop
LEFT JOIN public.role_definitions rd
  ON rd.org_id = aop.org_id AND rd.role_key = aop.role;
queries.detail_sql:
WITH admin_ops_pairs AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ur.org_id, ur.role
  FROM public.user_roles ur
  WHERE ur.role IN ('admin','ops')
)
SELECT aop.org_id, aop.role, (rd.id IS NOT NULL) AS definition_exists, rd.is_active
FROM admin_ops_pairs aop
LEFT JOIN public.role_definitions rd
  ON rd.org_id = aop.org_id AND rd.role_key = aop.role
WHERE rd.id IS NULL OR rd.is_active IS FALSE
ORDER BY aop.org_id, aop.role;
caveats: pairs_with_no_definition > 0 is the L2 lockout: M7 grants portal.access per role_definitions row, so an org whose memberships name admin/ops without a definition row receives no grant and loses the portal entirely at W-13 step 4.

pairs_defined_but_inactive is reported separately because an inactive definition may or may not be seeded a grant depending on M7's WHERE clause. Deciding that is W-13's job; Wave 0's job is to make sure the number is known rather than discovered.

result.answer: Yes. Every org holding an admin/ops membership has the matching, active role_definitions row.
result.verdict: The L2 lockout population is EMPTY, in both directions: no admin/ops (org, role) pair is undefined, and none is defined-but-inactive.
result.consequence: The plan §4 rule 'if Q5 > 0, W-13 gains a remediation step ahead of M7' DOES NOT FIRE. M7 can grant portal.access per role_definitions row and will miss no org. The §11 M7 preflight ('every org with an admin/ops membership receives the grant') is expected to pass unchanged.
result.note: pairs_defined_but_inactive = 0 also retires the open question of whether M7's WHERE clause should include inactive definitions. It is moot for this database — but M7 should still state its choice explicitly, because the answer would change if a definition is deactivated between now and the migration.

  count(DISTINCT p.org_id) AS orgs_affected
FROM public.user_access_profiles p

  AND EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM public.user_roles ur
    WHERE ur.user_id = p.user_id
      AND ur.org_id = p.org_id
      AND ur.role IN ('admin','ops')
  );

-- §4 announcement gate actually requires and what no artifact previously carried.

-- ** DO NOT paste this query's result back into this repository. ** It names a real person

SELECT

headline_finding.scale: The target database holds 2 orgs, 8 membership rows and 6 distinct (user, org) pairs. This is a pre-production-scale tenant.
headline_finding.implication_for_the_ritual: The §2 four-step switch ritual — seed, dual-read, prove zero across an observation window, switch — was designed for an UNKNOWN blast radius. At 6 pairs the blast radius is not merely known, it is exhaustively enumerable. A traffic-based observation window is the weaker instrument here: with this little traffic, 'zero divergences observed' is mostly evidence that nobody logged in. RECOMMENDATION: for this tenant, satisfy step 3 ('prove zero') by exhaustive enumeration of all 6 pairs — computing both the old and new answers for every one — rather than by observing divergences over a window. That is a stronger proof AND a cheaper one, and it dissolves the 'observation window is unspecified' limit recorded in plan §14.3 item 5. This is a recommendation to the workstream owners, not a unilateral change to the ritual.
headline_finding.caution: Small numbers reduce blast radius; they do not make the defects less real. The 2 fail-open pairs and the 1 silently-unrestricted admin are genuine, and the same code ships to any tenant that grows. W-5 (create path writes a profile) matters MORE at this scale, not less: it is what stops Q4 from growing the moment the product starts being used in earnest. Re-running this census before each lockout-class switch is cheap and is now a solved operation.
headline_finding.run_4_2026_09_04: THE PREDICTED GROWTH ARRIVED. This file's own caution — 'the 2 fail-open pairs are genuine, and W-5 is what stops Q4 from growing the moment the product starts being used in earnest' — is now measured rather than argued. The tenant went from 8 memberships over 6 pairs to 13 over 11, and pairs without an access profile went 2 -> 5. Three of the five new pairs arrived fail-open, so the create path is still not writing profiles and W-5 is accumulating the very backlog M1 must clear. Everything else held: no application trigger on auth.users, no legacy-only principals, no undefined roles, no undefined admin/ops definitions. The scale claim in `scale` above (2 orgs, 8 rows, 6 pairs) is superseded by run 4: 2 orgs, 13 rows, 11 pairs.

residual_risks: COUNTS ARE A SNAPSHOT, not an invariant. They now describe the database at 2026-08-07T17:24:15Z (run 3); the 2026-08-04 timestamp below is run 2's and is retained because the reasoning that follows was written against it and is unchanged by a third identical run — if anything a third zero-drift result makes the 'stability is not safety' point more strongly, not less. W-5 landed 2026-08-07 and closed the product membership writers, so Q4's growth path is shut, but run 3 does not demonstrate that: q4_membership_rows held at 8, so no membership was created and the writers were never exercised. Original text follows. They describe the database at 2026-08-04T17:00:21Z. Q4 in particular can GROW at any time, because the defect that produces it (W-5 — the create path writes no profile row) is still live: every membership created through POST /api/admin/users until W-5 ships adds another fail-open pair. Any lockout-class switch must re-run this census immediately before it, not cite this snapshot. That is now cheap via the trusted host action. NOTE: run 2 returning identical counts four days after run 1 is NOT evidence that the counts are stable — q4_membership_rows also held at 8, meaning no membership was created in the window. Zero drift here reflects zero activity, not a repaired defect, and must not be read as licence to skip the next re-run. UPDATED 2026-09-06 (asg_71201204af2de6) — THIS RISK IS NO LONGER HYPOTHETICAL AND ONE CLAIM ABOVE IS NOW DISPROVEN. The counts now describe the database at 2026-09-04T11:28:53Z (run 4). The sentence above — 'W-5 landed 2026-08-07 and closed the product membership writers, so Q4's growth path is shut' — IS FALSE AS A STATEMENT ABOUT THE TARGET. The growth path was not shut: Q4 grew 2 -> 5 in the following 28 days, and three of the five new (user, org) pairs arrived with no access profile. W-5 did close the ADMIN API path (POST /api/admin/users now RPCs create_membership_with_access_profile in one transaction, verified in source), so the claim was true about the route it named and false about the invariant it was read as establishing. run_4_root_cause_analysis identifies the writers that remain: seed and QA tooling that inserts into user_roles directly and that W-5's audit never covered. THE REUSABLE LESSON: this risk entry warned that three identical runs were evidence of an idle tenant rather than a fixed defect, and it was right — the fourth run is the one that moved. Do not let a run of stable censuses retire the standing instruction to re-run before any lockout-class switch.

runs_1_2_query_provenance.why_this_key_was_renamed: RENAMED FROM top-level `query_hash` 2026-08-07 by assignment asg_f34761f0f418ee, in the same edit that promoted run 3's amended SQL into combined_query. This rename is NOT cosmetic and MUST NOT be reverted while combined_query carries the target_identity block. trusted-host-action-registry.mjs:91-92 resolves the expected hash as `inputs.expectedQueryHash || j.query_hash`, then compares it to sha256(combined_query) and fails the run with `query_hash_mismatch` on any difference. A top-level key literally named `query_hash` holding 743cd63b… (the runs 1/2 hash) alongside the amended combined_query would therefore fail every run 3 attempt. With no key named `query_hash` and no key named `combined_query_hash`, expectedHash resolves to undefined, the comparison at :98 is skipped, and the registry computes and reports the hash itself — which is precisely what next_run_prepared.query_hash asks it to do.
runs_1_2_query_provenance.runs_1_2_remain_verifiable: Runs 1 and 2 stay fully verifiable, against a STRONGER anchor than a duplicated copy in this file. Their exact query bytes — together with their `results` block — are immutable in git at blob f95f89302bbd92f3e24e8c4a93dbb0231f0a664e, this file's content at commit 7dc06920a (the last commit before this edit). That blob's `combined_query` is the text whose sha256 is the 743cd63b… recorded above, and it is the text runs 1 and 2 actually executed. A transcribed second copy inside this file would have been weaker: it could be mistyped, and a mistyped copy would silently fail to hash to 743cd63b… while looking authoritative.

run_4_root_cause_analysis.what_that_rules_out: The product's own create path can no longer produce a fail-open pair. run_4_root_cause_analysis.what_this_census_CANNOT_say: Which of those paths created the three rows. Q4 reports counts, not rows, so attribution is beyond what was asked. Nor does this analysis establish what is DEPLOYED to the census target: W-5's closure is verified in this branch's source, and the target is alloy_deployed_primary. A branch that has W-5 and a deployment that does not would produce the same numbers.
run_4_root_cause_analysis.the_correction_to_the_earlier_diagnosis: Run 3's why_q4_did_not_grow blamed POST /api/admin/users ('still inserts into user_roles alone, route.ts:101-105'). That is no longer true of this branch — the fail-open insert is gone from the route. The mechanism that keeps Q4 refilling is therefore NOT the product create path but the seeding and QA tooling, which W-5 never covered and which M1 empties only until the next seed run. That is a different remediation from the one the plan currently carries.
run_4_root_cause_analysis.recommended_next_census: Add row-level attribution for the failing population only — (user_id, org_id, created_at, role) for pairs lacking a profile. Still read-only, still bounded, and it answers 'which path and when' in one run instead of by inference.
run_4_root_cause_analysis.recommended_workstream_change: W-5's scope should be read as 'no path creates a membership without a profile', not 'the admin API does not'. Either the seed/QA scripts adopt create_membership_with_access_profile, or the invariant is enforced in the database (a trigger, or the NOT NULL/FK that M9 contemplates) so that no writer can bypass it. Until one of those lands, M1 is a broom, not a fix.
